I.      INTRODUCTION

        On November 21, 2025, the Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate (PA OCA) and

the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate (DE DPA) submitted Joint Comments to the

Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANOPR) established in the above-captioned docket.1

The PA OCA represents the interests of Pennsylvania’s residential utility consumers, including

before the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC or Commission).2 The DE DPA

represents the interests of Delaware regulated utility consumers, including before FERC.3 The

Office of the Illinois Attorney General (IL OAG) represents the People of the State of Illinois on

public utility issues in proceedings before state and federal regulatory agencies and in state and

federal courts.4




1
  See generally, Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate Transmission System, Joint Comments of the
Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate and Delaware Division of the Public Advocate, Docket No. RM26-4-000
(Nov. 21, 2025). The Office of the Illinois Attorney General filed separate comments. See RM-26-4-000, Comments
of the People of the State of Illinois by the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (November 21, 2025).
2
  See 71 P.S. § 309-4 (outlining powers of Consumer Advocate to represent Pennsylvania’s residential utility
consumers in FERC proceedings and federal courts).
3
  See 29 Del. C. § 8716(e).
4
  See 15 ILCS 205/6.5(d).

                                                      1
         The PA OCA, DE DPA, and IL OAG (collectively, the Joint Consumer Advocates)

appreciate the opportunity to submit reply comments and further appreciates the DOE’s and

FERC’s efforts “to ensure all Americans and domestic industries have access to affordable,

reliable, and secure electricity.”5

        In submitting these reply comments, the Joint Consumer Advocates aim to protect the

interests of residential utility consumers by ensuring their access to a reliable and affordable

regional electricity grid. Residential ratepayers should not suffer unreliable electricity service or

pay unreasonably high rates for inferior, unreliable grid service as a result of the interconnection

of large loads that do not offset their demand through the addition of timely, local, and adequate

capacity resources.6

II.     SUMMARY OF REPLY COMMENTS

        FERC should adopt a cooperative federalism model to govern large load interconnections,

curtailments, and transmission cost allocations that preserves existing state jurisdiction. FERC

should clarify curtailment protocols within a cooperative federalism paradigm because new large

load growth may necessitate curtailments, and curtailments should protect current customers,

especially residential consumers, over new large load customers that cause the resource

inadequacy. The Joint Consumer Advocates are primarily concerned by the cumulative effect of

the undisciplined interconnection of new large loads during a time when market conditions indicate

that there may not be adequate generation capacity to serve all customers reliably.




5
   See U.S. Sec’y of Energy, Letter Communicating Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking on Large Load
Interconnection (Oct. 23, 2025), [hereinafter ANOPR] https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2025-
10/403%20Large%20Loads%20Letter.pdf.
6
  Joint Comments of the Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate and Delaware Division of the Public Advocate,
at pp. 2-3.

                                                      2
          Residential consumers, unlike new large loads, have paid capacity market rates for resource

adequacy, have not contributed to the growing grid resource inadequacy, and are not uniformly

able to mitigate the impact of curtailments through alternative supply options. To protect

residential consumers, FERC can and should recognize that RTOs must depart from pro-rata

transmission curtailment in the rare circumstances where (1) the large loads have caused the

resource inadequacy; and (2) the RTO (a) has exhausted all of its options for avoiding transmission

curtailment of customers, and (b) has established that those transmission customers that would be

disproportionately affected by the curtailment – large loads – have options to reduce their need for

transmission capacity, including alternative supply options, compensation for demand response,

or reduced transmission rates for the interruptible service they are provided.

         Given the unique issues that large loads create for grid reliability, treating new large loads

differently from other load is reasonable and necessary to ensure reliable service and just and

reasonable rates for existing consumers, especially residential consumers. FERC can and must

appropriately treat new large loads attributable to data centers differently from other kinds of load

because: (1) data centers are creating unique difficulties for the grid and impacting a uniquely

vulnerable market at a uniquely expensive level; and (2) investments in data centers can be

speculative and uncertain in nature, increasing the risk of a severe market correction that would

create stranded costs.7

         FERC should stay the course and adopt the proposed 20 MW threshold to define large loads

and hybrid facilities because this MW threshold helps protect against reliability concerns from




7
  See ADVAIT ARUN, BUBBLE OR NOTHING: DATA CENTER PROJECT FINANCE 43-48, 57-58, 60 (Ctr. for Pub. Enter.
2025), https://publicenterprise.org/report/bubble-or-nothing/ (describing the speculative nature of investment in new
large data center loads which creates a risk of stranded costs atypical under current market conditions).

                                                          3
 large loads or hybrid facilities by requiring proper interconnection studies that will reduce

reliability risks for all electricity consumers.

         Finally, FERC should build on FERC Order 2023 by continuing to streamline processes

that factor hybrid facilities jointly in the interconnection study. FERC should approach injection

and withdrawal rights according to grid-protective assumptions that prevent free-riding and

regulatory evasion. FERC and PJM should facilitate expedited interconnection studies of large

loads and hybrid facilities that agree to be meaningfully curtailable or dispatchable. FERC should

ensure that large loads and hybrid facilities pay fully for their network upgrade costs without

unjustly burdening residential ratepayers and all other grid users.

III.     REPLY COMMENTS

         A.       FERC should adopt a cooperative federalism model to govern large load
                  interconnections, curtailments, and transmission cost allocations.
                  1.     FERC should adopt a cooperative federalism model that preserves
                  existing state jurisdiction.

         FERC should adopt a cooperative federalism model to facilitate the interconnection of large

loads as retail customers directly through state jurisdictional facilities to interstate transmission

systems.8 Such an effort must preserve existing state authority according to the Federal Power Act

(FPA), as many commenters have emphasized.9 Cooperative federalism plays an important role

where state action furthers the objectives of the FPA and FERC, despite indirect effects on matters


8

with regulated entities and other stakeholders to explore consensus solutions for FERC’s consideration that will help
meet national goals for large load interconnection, while avoiding disputes over jurisdiction that would impede
achieving our shared goals.”). “Working together, under the concept of cooperative federalism, will lead to optimal
solutions.” Id.
9

Commissioners, at pp. 1-5; Comments of the Edison Electric Institute, at pp. 4, 22-32; Comments of PPL Services
Corporation, at pp. 8-9; Comments of Governor Josh Shapiro and Governor Glenn Youngkin, at p. 1.

 subject to FERC’s jurisdiction, while still expressing an important policy of the state. 10 However,

the Joint Consumer Advocates submit that further clarification is necessary regarding how

cooperative federalism applies to large load additions.

         Specifically, a regulatory framework of the “floor-not-ceiling” preemption model best suits

the careful balancing of interests that will enable FERC to achieve its goals and avoid burdensome

litigation.11 This framework is particularly important for setting federal minimum standards to

address grid reliability, including resource adequacy.12 These minimum standards must protect

residential customers13 by effectuating the FPA’s “‘core purposes’ of ‘curb[ing] prices and

enhanc[ing] reliability in the wholesale electricity market,’”14 while fully preserving state

regulatory jurisdiction over retail load interconnections and curtailments.15 Such minimum

standards should take two primary forms: (1) minimum, consumer-protective (pro forma) tariff

standards, terms, and conditions for Regional Transmission Operators (RTOs)/Independent System

Operators (ISOs) that will implement large load interconnection queues in coordination with

transmission owners (TOs) and interconnecting electric distribution companies (EDCs);16 and (2)

contractual agreements and cost allocations, such as transmission security agreements (TSAs)17

and construction services agreements.18

                  2.     FERC should clarify curtailment protocols within a cooperative
                  federalism paradigm because data center load growth may necessitate
                  curtailments, and curtailments should protect current customers over new
                  large data center load customers that cause resource inadequacy.

         Due to the harmful impact that the undisciplined addition of large loads to regional grids

has on resource adequacy and grid reliability, FERC and the states should cooperate to ensure that

the manual shedding of load, to the extent required, allocates the risk caused by such additions

without unduly discriminating against existing customers or creating unjust and unreasonable

capacity market paradigms. This is especially so for residential customers, which, unlike new large

loads, have paid capacity market rates for resource adequacy, have not contributed to the growing

resource inadequacy, and are not uniformly able to mitigate the impact of curtailments through

back-up supply options.19

Commission will increasingly be asked to review one-off agreements purporting to protect customers against

                                                           6
          FERC “has authority to effect orderly curtailment plans involving both direct sales and

sales for resale.”20 It also “has authority to curtail [transmission] deliveries to all customers in time

of shortage” without such curtailments interfering with the States’ exclusive authority over retail

sales.21 Indeed, RTOs have a vital role in allocating and administering curtailments.22

         But how exactly RTOs should administer large load curtailments within a cooperative

federalism paradigm requires the Commission’s clarification.23 To protect residential customers,

FERC can and should recognize that RTOs must depart from pro-rata transmission curtailment in

the rare circumstances where (1) the large loads have caused the resource inadequacy; and (2) the

RTO has (a) exhausted all of its options for avoiding transmission curtailment of customers, and

(b) has established that those transmission customers that would be disproportionately affected by

the curtailment – new large loads – have options to reduce their need for transmission capacity,

including alternative supply options, compensation for demand response, or reduced transmission

rates for the interruptible service they are provided.24

         B.       Given the unique issues that large loads create for grid reliability, treating new
                 large loads differently from other load is reasonable and necessary to ensure
                 reliable service and just and reasonable rates for existing consumers,
                 especially residential consumers.
        FERC and PJM should, when facilitating large load interconnections according to federal

priorities, make reasonable distinctions, meaning “due” discriminations, about data center load

because that load has unique characteristics that impact reliability and rates differently from other

loads.25 In fact, PJM’s initial Critical Issue Fast Path (CIFP) proposal for Large Load Additions

recognized the need to treat new large loads—nearly all of which are data centers26—differently

from other loads, by proposing to categorize them as Non-Capacity-Backed Load subject to

curtailment if they failed to bring their own generation or demand response.27 Although PJM

dropped the proposal,28 PJM’s Board and Staff introduced the initial proposal with differentiated

treatment for new large loads because they were looking squarely at the reality that new large data

center loads seek to interconnect in a regional grid projected to have insufficient capacity to

provide reliable service to its current customers.29

          customers. Id. (citing 16 U.S.C. § 824d(b)).

         PJM’s Independent Market Monitor (IMM) asserts that “[d]ata center load growth is the

primary reason for recent and expected capacity market conditions, including total forecast load

growth, the tight supply and demand balance, and high prices.”30 Moreover, in accepting its FERC-

approved temporary price collar, PJM acknowledged that it currently faces “extraordinary

circumstances . . . including rapid load growth, interconnection queue issues, a compressed auction

schedule, and significant unhedged load exposure.”31 Despite these unique, worrisome, and

potentially tragic conditions, data center load insists that PJM and FERC cannot treat these large

loads differently. But new large loads are different,32 and their effects on the market are different.33

        Google, for example, asserts that “[b]ecause all load is ‘economically marginal’ in the sense

that customers impose equivalent costs ‘whether by adding or merely continuing their usage’

regardless of when they first took service, imposing a requirement on only new load to bring its

own supply would be unjust and unreasonable and unduly discriminatory.”34 The case that Google

cites for this proposition, BNP Paribas Energy Trading GP v. FERC, implicitly assumes standard

additions of load in normal market conditions. In that case, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals

        Google implicitly equates data center loads under current market conditions to normal

loads in normal market conditions. With skyrocketing costs in PJM, the introduction of new large

loads causes a massive shift in the demand curve, a shift equal to the size of certain RTO markets.

The BNP Paribas court writes that “[w]here ‘all customers cause the incurrence of the costs . . . ,

whether by adding or merely continuing their usage,’ . . . assignment of the costs to all customers

(both continuing and new) forces each set ‘to weigh the marginal benefits of the capacity to them

against the marginal costs they impose on society by continuing to make demands.’”36 This

analysis of cost causation assumes that “all customers cause the incurrence of the costs,” which

does not capture the current economic and engineering realities of data centers’ outsized impact

on costs.37 Furthermore, the BNP Paribas court focuses on cost assignment’s role in causing

customers “to weigh the marginal benefits of the capacity to them against the marginal costs they

impose on society by continuing to make demands.”38 This marginal weighing, if it is to account

for current market conditions,39 should reflect the vast marginal costs that large new data centers

uniquely impose on other customers due to the necessary buildout of capacity to meet the demands

 of large loads while providing incumbent customers with adequate, reliable, and affordable

         Therefore, the Joint Consumer Advocates encourage FERC to reject a marginal view of

large load additions. Viewing each large load addition on an individual basis obfuscates the

cumulative pressure that undisciplined interconnection of large load customers creates. Instead,

FERC should view through a holistic lens the unique resource adequacy constraint which large

load additions can create if not properly mitigated. While a single large load addition may not—in

and of itself—create resource inadequacy, the totality of large load additions will. As a result, due

to the unique circumstances posed by current market conditions and the potential for the

undisciplined interconnection of large load customers, the Joint Consumer Advocates urge FERC

to view these additions on a cumulative basis.

          Further, new investment in large data center loads can be more speculative than that in

large loads which have already interconnected to the grid, increasing the risk of a severe market

correction that creates stranded costs; as a result, FERC and the states must adapt their regulations

to this new type of customer.41

         C.       Definition of Large Load and Hybrid Facilities
         In the ANOPR, the second principle for reform provides:

         Second, consistent with the Commission’s pro forma LGIP and LGIA, the reforms
         should only apply to new loads greater than 20 MW and, for hybrid facilities, where
         the load is greater than 20 MW. We seek comment on alternative thresholds,
         including whether such a threshold is necessary at all.42

         Several commenters assert that the 20 MW threshold for either new loads or hybrid

facilities is too low, arguing that it will clog interconnection queues and reduce opportunities for

streamlining the interconnection of these facilities.43

        The Joint Consumer Advocates disagree.44 The ANOPR definition applies to new large

load and hybrid facilities and therefore would not apply to commercial and industrial loads already

connected to lower voltage transmission lines.45
